img.tip: House seats follow the census; Michigan has 13 after the 2020 count.
img.title: COUNTED EVERY TEN YEARS

questions.question: Since a 2018 voter-approved amendment, who draws Michigan's legislative and congressional district maps?
questions.correctAnswer: An Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission - 13 citizens (4 Democrats, 4 Republicans, 5 unaffiliated) chosen partly by random selection from applicants
distractors: The Michigan Legislature, as in most of the state's history
The governor, with the advice of the Secretary of State
A panel of retired federal judges appointed by the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Proposal 2 of 2018 ('Voters Not Politicians') amended Article IV to take map-drawing away from legislators after decades of gerrymandering fights. The commission must draw by ranked criteria - equal population, the Voting Rights Act, contiguity, communities of interest - in public meetings.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Michigan voters fired the map-drawers and hired citizens instead.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of thirteen ordinary citizens around a table studying a large blank district map with colored pencils and transparent rulers, public-meeting room with folding chairs. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Michigan's maps are drawn by a 13-member Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission.
img.title: CITIZENS DRAW THE MAPS

questions.question: Which branch of government interprets the laws and settles disputes about what they mean?
questions.correctAnswer: To interpret the laws and decide cases and controversies under them
distractors: To enforce the laws with police and agencies
To write the laws for the nation
To collect the taxes that fund the government
questions.explanation: Article III vests 'the judicial Power of the United States' in the Supreme Court and the lower federal courts Congress creates. Interpreting law includes deciding whether laws conflict with the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Legislatures write it, executives carry it out, courts say what it means.

img.tip: The judicial branch interprets the laws and decides cases.
img.title: SAYING WHAT IT MEANS

questions.question: In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), the Supreme Court gave the Commerce Clause a broad reading. What did it hold?
questions.correctAnswer: Commerce includes navigation and commercial intercourse, and Congress's power over interstate commerce reaches activities crossing state lines
distractors: Commerce means only the buying and selling of goods at state borders
States may tax federal steamboat licenses
Congress may regulate only trade with foreign nations
questions.explanation: Marshall's Court held that New York could not grant a steamboat monopoly that excluded a federally licensed operator between New York and New Jersey. The broad definition of commerce later supported much of Congress's regulatory power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gibbons: commerce is intercourse, not just cargo.

img.tip: Gibbons v. Ogden read the Commerce Clause broadly - navigation counts.

questions.question: Which court stands at the top of the American judicial system, with the final word on the Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court of the United States
distractors: The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit
The US District Court for the District of Columbia
The chief justice's court of appeals
questions.explanation: Article III creates one Supreme Court; Congress has added lower federal courts beneath it. Its decisions on constitutional questions bind every other court in the country.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One court sits above all the others - the Supreme Court.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of the white marble Supreme Court building with its wide steps and columns, morning sun, visitors small on the plaza. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States.
img.title: THE HIGHEST COURT

questions.question: Judicial review - the power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution - traces to which early Supreme Court case?
questions.correctAnswer: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
distractors: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
questions.explanation: Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion held that a law conflicting with the Constitution is void and that 'it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' The case arose from a last-minute 'midnight judge' commission that was never delivered.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury is where judicial review was born - in a case the Court itself dismissed.

questions.question: Linda Brown's father challenged Topeka's segregated schools, and in 1954 a unanimous Supreme Court overturned the separate-but-equal doctrine in public education. What did the Court hold?
questions.correctAnswer: Racial segregation in public schools is unconstitutional - 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal'
distractors: Segregation is legal if facilities are truly equal
Only Southern states had to desegregate their schools
School assignments belong entirely to the states under the Tenth Amendment
questions.explanation: A unanimous Court overturned Plessy v. Ferguson's separate-but-equal doctrine in public education, holding that separating children by race stamps them with a badge of inferiority. Enforcement took years of further litigation and federal action.
questions.memoryHook: Brown: separate is inherently unequal.

questions.question: Police question a suspect in custody for hours without telling him of his rights; he confesses. Under Miranda v. Arizona (1966), the confession is generally:
questions.correctAnswer: Inadmissible - statements from custodial interrogation require prior warnings about silence and counsel
distractors: Admissible, because confessions are always voluntary if spoken aloud
Admissible only if two officers were present
Transferred to a military tribunal
questions.explanation: Miranda tied the Fifth Amendment's protection against self-incrimination and the Sixth Amendment right to counsel to police practice: suspects in custody must be warned they may remain silent, that statements can be used against them, and that they may have a lawyer, appointed if needed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: You have the right to remain silent - Miranda made them say it first.

questions.question: A protester burns an American flag outside a political convention and is convicted under a state flag-desecration law. Under Texas v. Johnson (1989), the conviction:
questions.correctAnswer: Is unconstitutional - flag burning as political protest is symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment
distractors: Stands, because the flag is exempt from the First Amendment
Stands, because burning anything in public is arson
Is sent to Congress for a final decision
questions.explanation: By 5-4, the Court held that the government may not prohibit expression simply because society finds it offensive. Congress's later Flag Protection Act was struck down on the same reasoning in United States v. Eichman.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Johnson: even burning the flag can be protected speech - that is the price of the First Amendment.

questions.question: After Citizens United v. FEC (2010), which kind of political spending by corporations and unions became constitutionally protected without limits?
questions.correctAnswer: Corporations and unions may spend unlimited amounts independently supporting or opposing candidates, because independent expenditures are protected speech
distractors: Corporations may donate unlimited money directly to candidates
All campaign finance laws were repealed
Only individual citizens may spend money in elections
questions.explanation: The Court distinguished independent expenditures (protected, unlimited) from direct contributions (still limitable, and corporate contributions to candidates remain banned). Disclosure requirements were upheld. The decision opened the era of super PACs.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Citizens United: independent spending is speech; direct giving is still limited.

questions.question: A federal criminal case begins, is appealed, and may end at the Supreme Court. What is the correct ladder of courts?
questions.correctAnswer: US District Court (trial) -> US Court of Appeals (circuit) -> US Supreme Court
distractors: US Court of Appeals -> US District Court -> US Supreme Court
State supreme court -> US District Court -> US Senate
US District Court -> state circuit court -> US Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The 94 district courts are the trial courts of the federal system. Their decisions appeal to one of the regional circuit courts of appeals (plus the Federal Circuit), and the Supreme Court chooses a small share of cases by granting certiorari - four justices must agree to hear a case.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: District tries it, circuit reviews it, the Supreme Court picks its few.

questions.question: A child is born in Detroit to parents who are citizens of another country, and is raised in Michigan. Under the Fourteenth Amendment, that child is:
questions.correctAnswer: A citizen of the United States from birth (the Citizenship Clause covers all persons born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction)
distractors: Not a citizen until naturalized as an adult
A citizen of the parents' country only
A citizen only after passing a civics test at age 18
questions.explanation: The Citizenship Clause reversed Dred Scott by writing birthright citizenship into the Constitution. Children born on US soil are citizens regardless of their parents' status, with narrow historical exceptions such as children of foreign diplomats.
questions.memoryHook: Born here means citizen here - the Fourteenth Amendment says so.

img.tip: Born or naturalized in the United States: a citizen.
img.title: CITIZEN BY BIRTH

questions.question: Which set lists real requirements for naturalization as a US citizen?
questions.correctAnswer: Lawful permanent residence for the required years, good moral character, English and civics knowledge, and an oath of allegiance
distractors: Military service, property ownership and a college degree
Birth in a US territory and ten years of taxes paid
A sponsor who is a senator, plus a public examination in state history
questions.explanation: Federal law (the Immigration and Nationality Act) requires most applicants to be lawful permanent residents (usually five years, three if married to a citizen), show good moral character, pass English and civics tests, and take the oath renouncing foreign allegiances.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Residence, character, English, civics, oath - the five gates to naturalization.

img.tip: Naturalization: residence, good moral character, English and civics, and the oath.

questions.question: Serving on a jury when called is a duty that applies to whom?
questions.correctAnswer: Citizens - it is one of the legal duties that only citizens bear (along with voting rights, noncitizens never serve on US juries)
distractors: All residents, including visitors on tourist visas
Only citizens who own property
Only lawyers and judges
questions.explanation: Jury service is drawn from citizen rolls such as voter and driver records. Together with obeying the law and paying taxes (which bind everyone present), jury duty is distinctively a citizen's duty - and the mechanism that makes the Sixth Amendment's jury right real.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The jury box is filled by citizens - that is why the summons matters.

img.tip: Jury duty is a legal duty of citizens.
img.title: TWELVE CITIZENS

questions.question: What is the main job of a political party?
questions.correctAnswer: To nominate candidates and win elections so it can organize and run the government
distractors: To count ballots and certify results
To write laws directly as private organizations
To fund the courts
questions.explanation: Parties recruit and nominate candidates, campaign to win offices, and then organize legislatures and executives. Election administration itself belongs to government officials, not parties.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties exist to win power through elections - everything else is support.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a campaign headquarters with volunteers at phones and folding tables, a candidate shaking hands at the door, energetic but orderly mood. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Parties nominate candidates and try to win elections and govern.
img.title: WIN TO GOVERN

questions.question: A teachers' union hires lobbyists to push for school funding but runs no candidates of its own, while an organization across town recruits candidates for every office. What key difference between interest groups and political parties does this illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: Interest groups try to influence policy without seeking to govern; parties try to win office and govern
distractors: Interest groups are illegal, while parties are constitutional
Interest groups run candidates under their own names in general elections
There is no real difference between them
questions.explanation: A union, a business association or a citizens' league lobbies, publicizes and litigates to move policy on its issues - but it does not nominate a full slate to run the government. Parties do. Madison anticipated both in Federalist No. 10's discussion of factions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties want the wheel; interest groups want to lean on the driver.

questions.question: News organizations investigate officials, publish their findings and criticize policy freely. Which democratic role is this?
questions.correctAnswer: The watchdog role of a free press - it informs citizens and holds power accountable between elections
distractors: The propaganda role required by the First Amendment
The judicial role of the fourth branch, with power to remove officials
A violation of the separation of powers
questions.explanation: A free press cannot remove anyone, but exposure changes politics: investigations inform voters, deter corruption and force responses. The First Amendment's press clause protects this checking function - sometimes called the 'fourth estate.'
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The press cannot fire officials - it hands the evidence to the voters.

questions.question: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argues that a large republic controls factions better than a small one because:
questions.correctAnswer: A large republic contains more diverse interests, making it harder for any unjust majority faction to form and act together
distractors: Large republics can outlaw all political parties
Distance makes citizens too apathetic to organize
A large republic lets the Senate veto all faction proposals
questions.explanation: Madison defined a faction as citizens united by a passion or interest adverse to others' rights. Since factions cannot be eliminated without destroying liberty, the extended republic filters and dilutes them - representatives refine public views, and many competing interests check each other.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Madison's cure for factions is more factions, spread wider.

questions.question: Besides voting, which is a way citizens can take part in government?
questions.correctAnswer: Contacting elected officials, joining a party or campaign, attending public meetings, or petitioning the government
distractors: Refusing to pay taxes until policies change
Serving in the legislature without being elected
Nullifying laws they personally dislike
questions.explanation: Participation runs from writing a representative, to volunteering, to running for office. In Michigan, citizens also wield direct tools - initiative, referendum and recall - that most Americans lack in such strong form.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Voting is the floor of citizenship, not the ceiling.

img.tip: Citizens can contact officials, campaign, attend meetings and petition.
img.title: MORE THAN VOTING

questions.question: What is the purpose of a primary election, as compared with a general election?
questions.correctAnswer: A primary chooses each party's nominee; the general election chooses the officeholder among the nominees
distractors: A primary is for federal offices only; a general election is for state offices
A primary is held by the courts; a general election is held by the parties
They are the same event in odd and even years
questions.explanation: Michigan holds its state primary in August of even years and the general election in November. In Michigan's presidential primary, voters must tell the clerk which party's ballot they want (a record kept for that election), while regular primaries use a single ballot with separate party columns.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Primaries pick the fighters; the general picks the winner.

questions.question: An elector in the Electoral College votes for a different candidate than the one who won her state's popular vote. May the state punish her for it?
questions.correctAnswer: Yes - in Chiafalo v. Washington (2020) the Court unanimously upheld state laws penalizing 'faithless electors'

Only if Congress passes a law for that election
Yes, but only in the first Electoral College vote in history
questions.explanation: States appoint electors in the manner their legislatures direct, and most bind them by pledge. Washington fined faithless electors from 2016; the Court held that the power to appoint includes the power to require and enforce the pledge.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Electors are messengers the state can bind - Chiafalo made it unanimous.

questions.question: Washington's Supreme Court seats nine. Lansing's highest court is smaller - how many justices serve on the Michigan Supreme Court?
questions.correctAnswer: Seven justices, including one chosen by the court itself as chief justice
distractors: Nine, the same as the US Supreme Court
Five justices
Twelve justices
questions.explanation: Article VI, Section 2 of the Michigan Constitution fixes the court at seven justices serving eight-year terms. The court sits in the Michigan Hall of Justice in Lansing, across from the Capitol.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Seven in Lansing, nine in Washington - do not mix them up.

questions.question: Michigan Supreme Court justices appear on the nonpartisan section of the ballot. How do candidates get there?
questions.correctAnswer: They are nominated at political party conventions (or by petition), then elected statewide in the nonpartisan general election for eight-year terms
distractors: They are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Senate
They are chosen by the other justices for life
They are elected in partisan primaries like legislators
questions.explanation: Michigan's system is a hybrid unique in its details: parties nominate judicial candidates at conventions, incumbents may file an affidavit of candidacy, but the general-election ballot lists judicial races without party labels. Justices serve eight-year terms, and no one may be elected or appointed to a judicial office after reaching the age of 70 (Article VI, Section 19) - a justice elected before turning 70 may serve out the full term.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nominated by parties, elected without party labels - Michigan's judicial twist.

questions.question: Michigan's constitution declares that its courts form 'one court of justice.' What does that phrase organize?
questions.correctAnswer: A single unified court system: the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals, trial courts (circuit courts and their counterparts) and district courts, under the Supreme Court's superintending control
distractors: A merger of state and federal courts into one building
One single courthouse for the entire state in Lansing
The abolition of all trial courts below the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Article VI, Section 1 vests the judicial power in 'one court of justice' composed of the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals (created by the 1963 Constitution), circuit courts as the general-jurisdiction trial courts, and other courts the legislature establishes, such as district and probate courts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One court of justice - many courtrooms, one system.

questions.question: Which list correctly names the local governments that organize daily life in Michigan under Article VII?
questions.correctAnswer: Counties, townships (including charter townships), cities and villages - with cities and villages empowered to adopt home-rule charters
distractors: Provinces, prefectures and parishes
Only counties - Michigan has no other local units
School districts and water districts only
questions.explanation: Michigan has 83 counties and more than 1,200 townships; charter townships and home-rule cities and villages frame their own charters within state law. Article VII also limits how these units tax and borrow, keeping local power close but bounded.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Counties, townships, cities, villages - Michigan is governed locally, too.

questions.question: What did Michigan's Headlee Amendment (1978) do to state and local taxation?
questions.correctAnswer: It capped state revenue growth, required voter approval for new local taxes, and barred the state from shifting its funding duties onto local governments without paying
distractors: It abolished the state income tax
It let local governments raise any tax without a vote
It federalized Michigan's tax system
questions.explanation: Voters added the Headlee provisions (Article IX, Sections 25-34) after the tax revolts of the 1970s: if state revenue outgrows personal income, the excess is refunded; local units need voter approval to levy new taxes; and Lansing cannot mandate new local services without funding them. A related rule: Article IX, Section 7 forbids a graduated income tax - Michigan's income tax must stay flat.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Headlee put the taxpayers' hand on the tax tap.

questions.question: Why does Michigan's constitution contain detailed policy rules - tax limits, a trust fund for land, a redistricting commission - that the US Constitution leaves out?
questions.correctAnswer: State constitutions are meant to limit and direct state governments in detail, and they are far easier to amend, so generations of voters have written current policy concerns into them
distractors: Because the US Constitution secretly requires states to copy federal policy
Because Michigan's constitution was written by Congress
Because the federal courts ordered Michigan to add them
questions.explanation: The federal charter is a grant of powers to a government of limited jurisdiction; a state constitution is mainly a limit on a government of general power. With amendments available by simple voter majority (and by petition), Michigan voters repeatedly chose constitutional - not merely statutory - protection for their priorities.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Easy to amend means policy moves in - that is the story of state constitutions.

questions.question: Why does Michigan have its own constitution at all, instead of simply living under the US Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism - each state organizes its own government, courts and local units, and Michigan's constitution is the charter that does it
distractors: Because Michigan was once a separate country by treaty
Because the US Constitution applies only to states east of the Mississippi
Because the President granted Michigan a charter in 1837
questions.explanation: The US Constitution governs the federal sphere and sets a floor of rights; it does not design Michigan's legislature, courts, townships or tax rules. Michigan's own constitution does that work - and can protect rights beyond the federal floor.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two constitutions, two jobs - every Michigander lives under both.

questions.question: The Fourteenth Amendment opens: 'All persons born or naturalized in the United States... are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they reside.' What big idea does that sentence state?
questions.correctAnswer: Dual citizenship - every American holds national and state citizenship at once, with rights protected at both levels
distractors: Citizens must choose one citizenship at age 18
State citizenship replaces national citizenship inside state borders
Only native-born persons hold both citizenships
questions.explanation: An American in Lansing is simultaneously a citizen of the United States and of Michigan. Each citizenship carries its own rights and duties - federal courts and the US Constitution at one level, Michigan's Declaration of Rights and courts at the other - and the Fourteenth Amendment forbids states to abridge the national privileges or immunities.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One person, two citizenships - that is the American design.
